title: Trump Commutes Lenora Logan’s Sentence for Crack Cocaine Conspiracy
description_medium: On October 21, 2020, Trump commuted Lenora Logan’s federal sentence for conspiring to distribute and possess with intent to distribute crack cocaine. DOJ lists an amended 324-month prison term and ten years of supervised release, imposed in 1999. The commutation reduced the prison sentence; it did not pardon the conviction. The White House said Alice Marie Johnson advocated for Logan’s clemency.
description_long:
President Donald Trump commuted Lenora Logan’s sentence on October 21, 2020. The Justice Department identifies Logan’s case in the Southern District of Iowa and records a conviction for conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute cocaine base, commonly called crack. Her sentence was 324 months in prison, as amended, followed by ten years of supervised release; sentencing occurred on December 30, 1999.

The commutation changed the prison portion of the sentence, while leaving the conviction and other sentence terms in place. The White House announcement presented the action among five commutations and said Alice Marie Johnson, whose own life sentence Trump had earlier commuted, advocated on Logan’s behalf. The available official listing does not explain Logan’s role in the conspiracy or describe its scale, so those details are not inferred. The event is one of several 2020 grants connected to Johnson’s clemency advocacy and illustrates the difference between shortening imprisonment and granting a pardon.
evidence_notes: Official DOJ index supports offense, term, court and sentencing date; White House statement confirms Oct. 21 action and Johnson’s advocacy.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Commutes Lenora Logan’s Sentence for Crack Cocaine Conspiracy

title: Trump Commutes Charles Tanner’s Cocaine Conspiracy Sentence
description_medium: Trump commuted Charles Tanner’s federal sentence on October 21, 2020. DOJ records a cocaine-distribution conspiracy conviction in Indiana and an original 360-month term, later amended, plus ten years’ supervised release and a fine. Tanner had served about 16 years of a 30-year sentence. The White House said Alice Marie Johnson advocated for him; the grant reduced imprisonment without pardoning the conviction.
description_long:
On October 21, 2020, President Donald Trump commuted Charles Tanner’s sentence for a federal cocaine-distribution conspiracy. The Justice Department’s clemency index lists the Northern District of Indiana and a 360-month prison term, as amended, followed by ten years of supervised release and a $1,000 fine. The White House described Tanner as a former professional boxer who had served about 16 years of a 30-year sentence and participated in education and reentry programming in prison.

The clemency announcement said Alice Marie Johnson, herself a previous Trump clemency recipient, advocated for Tanner. A commutation reduces a sentence; it does not pardon the conviction or determine that the underlying case was invalid. The sentence listing and White House statement support the action and relevant context, but the public announcement does not provide a detailed account of Tanner’s conduct within the conspiracy. That distinction keeps the description focused on the documented case and the clemency decision.
evidence_notes: DOJ lists original amended sentence terms; White House/AP coverage says Tanner had served about 16 of 30 years and identifies Alice Johnson’s advocacy.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Commutes Charles Tanner’s Cocaine Conspiracy Sentence

title: Trump Pardons Utah Commissioner Phil Lyman for Recapture Canyon Ride
description_medium: Trump pardoned Utah state representative Phillip “Phil” Kay Lyman on December 22, 2020, for misdemeanor convictions arising from an off-road vehicle ride into Recapture Canyon, an area closed to motorized vehicles to protect archaeological resources. DOJ records 36 months’ probation, ten days’ incarceration, a $1,000 fine and $95,955.61 restitution. The White House called the prosecution selective; the pardon did not erase the convictions.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted Phillip Kay “Phil” Lyman a full pardon on December 22, 2020, for federal misdemeanor convictions tied to a 2014 off-road vehicle ride in Recapture Canyon, southeastern Utah. The canyon was closed to motorized traffic to protect archaeological and cultural resources. Lyman, then a San Juan County commissioner, organized a group ride that he characterized as a protest against federal land restrictions. A federal jury convicted him of conspiracy and operating an off-road vehicle on closed public land.

The Justice Department records a sentence of 36 months’ probation, including ten days in custody, a $1,000 fine and $95,955.61 in restitution. Lyman was a Utah state representative when Trump pardoned him. The White House said he had been selectively prosecuted, a position Lyman and supporters advanced; the conviction remained part of the historical court record. Contemporary Utah reporting documents the ride, the site’s protections and the clemency. The pardon was therefore politically salient in debates about public-land access and enforcement, while its legal effect was limited to forgiving Lyman’s federal offenses.
evidence_notes: Used official clemency record plus Utah reporting on Recapture Canyon. Clarified that pardon was Dec. 22, 2020, and convictions were misdemeanors tied to the closed-canyon ride.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Pardons Utah Commissioner Phil Lyman for Recapture Canyon Ride

title: Trump Pardons Utah Man Lynn Wade Barney for Felon-in-Possession Conviction
description_medium: Trump granted Lynn Wade Barney a full pardon on January 13, 2021, for possessing a firearm and ammunition as a person previously convicted of a felony. DOJ lists a 35-month prison sentence and three years of supervised release in the District of Utah. The offense was separate from the earlier felony that barred him from possessing firearms. Public sources establish the pardon and case basics but provide little context about the underlying possession.
description_long:
On January 13, 2021, President Donald Trump granted Lynn Wade Barney a full pardon for a federal conviction in the District of Utah. The Justice Department’s clemency record identifies the offense as possession of a firearm and ammunition by a person previously convicted of a felony. Barney received 35 months in prison and three years of supervised release after a 2005 conviction. The earlier felony conviction made firearm possession unlawful; available public records do not provide enough detail to describe the particular firearm or circumstances of possession.

The pardon forgave the federal conviction but did not erase its history. It also did not turn the pardon into a finding about the validity of either case. The official warrant establishes the clemency date and case, while the public explanation is limited. Keeping that boundary clear avoids adding unsupported details about the firearm or the prior offense. Barney’s case was among a large set of last-day pardons and commutations issued in January 2021, but the fact of being part of a broader grant list does not itself explain why he was selected.
evidence_notes: Official DOJ index and pardon warrant support January 13, 2021 date, district, offense and sentence. Left individual conduct unspecified because public documentation located was limited.

title: Trump Pardons Oklahoma Gun Dealer Fred Keith Alford for 1977 Firearms Violation
description_medium: Trump granted Fred Keith Alford a full pardon on January 19, 2021, for a 1977 federal firearms violation involving an interstate sale by a licensed firearms dealer. DOJ records one year of unsupervised probation. The White House states that this was Alford’s only conviction. The decades-old pardon forgave the offense but does not establish that the underlying law or conviction was invalid.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted Fred Keith Alford a full pardon on January 19, 2021, for a federal firearms offense dating to 1977. The Justice Department identifies the conviction in the Northern District of Oklahoma as an interstate sale of a firearm by a federal firearms licensee and records a sentence of one year of unsupervised probation. The White House described Alford as having been convicted for a firearms violation and said he served that probation without supervision.

The case was decades old by the time clemency was granted. The pardon forgave the federal conviction; it did not erase the historical case or show that the conviction was legally unsound. Public materials reviewed here do not provide the circumstances of the sale or identify the firearm, so the account should not go further. The clemency is notable chiefly for its age and the nature of the offense, rather than for a documented policy campaign or detailed public explanation.
evidence_notes: DOJ official listing supplies federal offense and probation term; White House says Alford was convicted in 1977 and served one year’s unsupervised probation.

title: Trump Pardons Oregon Rancher Steven Hammond for Federal Arson Convictions
description_medium: Trump pardoned Oregon rancher Steven Dwight Hammond on July 10, 2018, for two convictions of using fire to damage federal property. The fires occurred in 2001 and 2006 on public lands where the family ran cattle; the 2006 fire was in Malheur National Wildlife Refuge. His sentence had been increased to five years under the mandatory minimum. The pardon ended the federal punishment but did not erase the convictions.
description_long:
On July 10, 2018, President Donald Trump pardoned Oregon rancher Steven Dwight Hammond for two federal convictions of using fire to damage government property. A jury found that Hammond and his father, Dwight, set the 2001 Hardie-Hammond fire on federal grazing land; Steven was also convicted for a 2006 fire at the Krumbo Butte area of the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge. Both fires burned federal land used in connection with the family’s cattle ranching.

The Justice Department’s clemency record lists the original sentence of 12 months and one day, later increased to five years under the federal mandatory-minimum provision, plus supervised release. The White House said the Hammonds were multi-generation ranchers and described the fire as spreading onto a small portion of neighboring public grazing land. The pardon forgave the convictions but did not change the court verdict or the underlying land-management disputes. The case became nationally prominent after the Hammonds’ return to prison helped prompt an armed occupation of the Malheur refuge by anti-government activists in 2016; that occupation was a separate event and should not be conflated with the arson convictions.
evidence_notes: Separated the Hammonds’ federal fire convictions from the later Malheur occupation. DOJ charging and clemency records establish fires, counts, sentence and pardon date.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Pardons Oregon Rancher Steven Hammond for Federal Arson Convictions

title: Trump Pardons Former Congressman Chris Collins in Insider-Trading Case
description_medium: Trump pardoned former New York congressman Christopher Carl Collins on December 22, 2020, for conspiracy to commit securities fraud and making false statements. Collins had tipped his son about negative trial results at an Australian biotechnology company, allowing relatives to sell shares before the news became public. His 26-month prison sentence, one year of supervised release and $200,000 fine were part of the case. His son was not pardoned.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted former Republican congressman Christopher Carl Collins a full pardon on December 22, 2020. Collins had pleaded guilty in 2019 to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and making false statements. Prosecutors said he learned that Innate Immunotherapeutics, an Australian biotechnology company in which he was a major investor and board member, had failed a drug trial, then relayed the information to his son before it became public. Collins’s son and other relatives sold shares, avoiding losses as the company’s stock fell after disclosure.

The Justice Department lists a 26-month prison sentence, one year of supervised release and a $200,000 fine. Collins resigned from Congress before entering his plea. His son Cameron Collins separately pleaded guilty and was not included in Trump’s pardon. The case joined political power and private financial interests: Collins was a sitting representative when the tip occurred. The pardon forgave Collins’s federal offenses but did not erase the case record or extend to other participants. The official record and contemporaneous reporting support these distinctions.
evidence_notes: DOJ clemency index confirms offense and sentence; SDNY case announcement describes the insider-trading sequence and sentence. Clarifies his son was not pardoned.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Pardons Former Congressman Chris Collins in Insider-Trading Case

title: Trump Pardons Former Pittsburgh Dentist Alfonso Costa for Health Care Fraud
description_medium: Trump pardoned Alfonso Antonio Costa on December 22, 2020, for health care fraud tied to fraudulent oral-surgery billing. The former Pittsburgh dentist pleaded guilty in 2007. DOJ lists three years’ probation, including a year of home confinement, 100 hours of community service, a $250,000 fine and $44,579.47 restitution. The White House identified HUD Secretary Ben Carson and former NFL player Jerome Bettis among those supporting his pardon.
description_long:
On December 22, 2020, President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Alfonso Antonio Costa, a former Pittsburgh-area dentist convicted of health care fraud. Costa pleaded guilty in 2007 to submitting fraudulent claims for oral surgery services. The Justice Department records that he was sentenced in 2008 to three years’ probation, including one year of home confinement, 100 hours of community service, a $250,000 fine and $44,579.47 restitution.

The White House said Housing and Urban Development Secretary Ben Carson and former Pittsburgh Steelers player Jerome Bettis supported Costa’s clemency request, and described Costa’s later community service. Contemporary Pittsburgh reporting described the billing case and sentencing. Costa’s pardon forgave the conviction but did not eliminate the historical record or establish that the sentence had been improper. His case drew attention because the White House announced support from a cabinet secretary who was also a friend and business associate. That connection is relevant context for the grant, while the criminal case itself concerned false oral-surgery billing.
evidence_notes: Corrected context using DOJ clemency record, White House support statement and Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reporting on Costa’s actual billing offense.

title: Trump Pardons Oklahoma Man Alfred Lee Crum for 1952 Moonshine Case
description_medium: Trump granted Alfred Lee Crum a full pardon on December 22, 2020, for a 1952 moonshine offense in Oklahoma. Crum, then 19, pleaded guilty to helping his wife’s uncle illegally distill alcohol and received three years’ probation. The White House said it was his only criminal case and described his long community and family life. The pardon forgave the conviction, nearly seven decades later.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted Alfred Lee Crum a full pardon on December 22, 2020, for a federal moonshine offense from 1952. The White House said Crum was 19 when he pleaded guilty to helping his wife’s uncle illegally distill alcohol in Oklahoma. The Justice Department’s clemency warrant records the pardon; contemporaneous coverage says the offense resulted in three years of probation and was his only criminal case.

The White House emphasized the extraordinary time between the conviction and pardon, describing Crum’s long marriage, church attendance, family life and community fundraising. Those details were part of the official explanation for clemency, not facts about the underlying distilling case. The pardon forgave the old federal conviction but did not erase the historical record. Crum’s case differs from clemency for currently incarcerated people: the public account concerns a decades-old conviction followed by a long period without further criminal cases. The official pardon statement and contemporary reports support that summary without adding claims about the scale of the distilling operation.
evidence_notes: Corrected unsupported generic record with the official White House announcement’s specific account and DOJ pardon warrant.
